[IBNABIHATIM:v3p868/r2] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · عائشة | reports | A poor guardian who cares for an orphan may take a reasonable amount.
[IBNABIHATIM:v3p868/r3] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · النبي ﷺ | reports | The Prophet permits a poor caretaker reasonable, non-excessive use when asked what he may take.
[IBNABIHATIM:v3p868/r4] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · ابن عباس | reports | One report limits the guardian's eating to three fingers.
[IBNABIHATIM:v3p868/r5] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · الحسن | reports | A poor guardian serving the orphans may eat from the edges of their estate.
[IBNABIHATIM:v3p868/r6] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · عائشة، أبو العالية | reports | Another view allows eating in proportion to the work done for the orphan.
[IBNABIHATIM:v3p868/r7] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · ابن عباس، مجاهد، ميمون بن مهران، الحكم | reports | An alternative is for a poor guardian to live on his own means rather than use the orphan's wealth.
[IBNABIHATIM:v3p869/r1] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · ابن عباس، عبيدة، أبو العالية، أبو وائل، سعيد بن جبير، مجاهد، الضحاك، السدي | reports | One interpretation permits a poor guardian to borrow from the orphan's property.
[IBNABIHATIM:v3p869/r2] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · سعيد بن جبير | reports | A loan may cover basic sustenance; repay if solvent, but dying insolvent brings no sin, and this is the only exception.
[IBNABIHATIM:v3p869/r3] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · سعيد بن جبير، السدي، مجاهد، أبو وائل | reports | Another loan view says a dying guardian should seek release from the orphan or his guardian; if unable to repay, God may absolve him.
[IBNABIHATIM:v3p869/r4] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · إبراهيم | reports | A customary allowance is enough to satisfy hunger and cover nakedness, not fine linen clothing.
[IBNABIHATIM:v3p869/r5] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · إبراهيم، عطية، عطاء، عكرمة، الحسن | reports | A different view allows taking from the estate without repayment.
[IBNABIHATIM:v3p870/r1] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · الشعبي | reports | The guardian may take only under necessity comparable to carrion and must repay it.
[IBNABIHATIM:v3p870/r2] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · يحيى بن سعيد، ربيعة | reports | Alternatively, a poor orphan may receive support according to his poverty, with nothing going to the guardian.
[IBNABIHATIM:v3p870/r3] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · ابن أبي الزناد | reports | The allowance for a poor person applies specifically to Bedouins and their like.
[IBNABIHATIM:v3p870/r4] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · سعيد بن جبير | reports | The command to hand over property is addressed to trustees.
[IBNABIHATIM:v3p870/r5] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · ابن عباس | reports | Trustees should deliver the orphan's property with witnesses, as God commanded.
[IBNABIHATIM:v3p870/r6] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · سعيد بن جبير | reports | Trustees deliver the property when the orphans reach puberty.
[IBNABIHATIM:v3p871/r1] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · سعيد بن جبير | reports | God is sufficient as witness and no witness is better between trustees and orphans.
[NAHHAS:v1p437/r1] NAHHAS, d. 338 · أبو عبد الرحمن السلمي | reports | Abu Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami reads رشدا; رشدا and رشد are verbal nouns of رشد, as is الرشاد.
[NAHHAS:v1p437/r2] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | إسرافا is either a purpose object or a verbal noun functioning circumstantially; بدارا is coordinated with it, and أن يكبروا is governed by بدار.
[NAHHAS:v1p437/r3] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | If the guardian is wealthy, he should abstain; if poor, he may eat reasonably; witnessing follows handing over the orphans’ property.
[NAHHAS:v1p437/r4] NAHHAS, d. 338 · الخليل وسيبويه | reports | Al-Khalil and Sibawayh allow إذا as a conditional in poetry, where it requires a verbal answer, but not in prose because its following clause is settled.
[THALABI:v3p243/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · عطاء | reports | Ata warns a guardian not to make a profit from the orphan in his care, who is still naïve and young.
[THALABI:v3p243/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · مجاهد وباذان | reports | Mujahid and Badan warn against hastening unlawful income before lawful provision arrives.
[THALABI:v3p254/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | Ibn Masud's codex has أحستم, equivalent to أحسستم with one of two identical sīn letters omitted, as in a Qurʾanic form and a cited poem. | mentions 56:65
[THALABI:v3p254/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · السلمي وعيسى | reports | Al-Sulami and Isa read رُشْدا with fatḥa on rāʾ and shīn; the common reading uses a different vowel pattern.
[THALABI:v3p254/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · المفسرون | reports | The commentators define discernment as sound judgment, personal integrity, safeguarding wealth, and knowing how to manage it.
[THALABI:v3p254/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · سعيد بن جبير ومجاهد والشعبي | reports | Saʿid ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, and al-Shaʿbi say guardians sometimes withheld an orphan's assets despite his maturity until they recognized his sound judgment.
[THALABI:v3p254/r5] THALABI, d. 427 · الضحاك | reports | Al-Dahhak says an orphan must not be given his property even at one hundred years old until his competence in managing it is established.
[THALABI:v3p254/r6] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | Removal of legal restraint and delivery of a minor orphan's property require both puberty and discernment, after the guardian has tested the child.
[THALABI:v3p254/r7] THALABI, d. 427 · جماعة من الفقهاء | reports | Jurists test a boy by assigning household spending or a small sum to manage, and a girl by entrusting household management and supervised spinning; the incompetent remain under restraint.
[THALABI:v3p254/r8] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | One puberty sign shared by men and women is ejaculation, whether through intercourse, a wet dream, or otherwise; the author cites the command that children who reach puberty ask permission. | mentions 24:59
[THALABI:v3p254/r9] THALABI, d. 427 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The Prophet's instruction to Muadh in Yemen to collect a dinar from each ḥālim is cited as evidence that ejaculation marks legal adulthood.
[THALABI:v3p255/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · الشافعي وأبو يوسف ومحمد | reports | Al-Shafiʿi, Abu Yusuf, and Muhammad recognize puberty at fifteen years or upon pubic hair growth.
[THALABI:v3p255/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · أبو حنيفة | reports | Abu Hanifa sets a girl's age of puberty at seventeen, with two reports for a boy: nineteen as the more common position, or eighteen.
[THALABI:v3p255/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · مالك وداود | reports | Malik and Dawud reject age alone as a puberty marker; Dawud requires ejaculation even at forty, while Malik uses a deepened voice or a changed nose.
[THALABI:v3p255/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · عبد الله بن عمر | reports | Ibn Umar says the Prophet rejected him for fighting at fourteen but accepted him at fifteen, supporting fifteen as the age of puberty.
[THALABI:v3p255/r5] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | Pubic hair means coarse hair around the genitals; al-Shafiʿi has two views, that it constitutes adulthood or merely indicates it, while Abu Hanifa gives it no legal effect.
[THALABI:v3p255/r6] THALABI, d. 427 · عطية القرظي | reports | Atiyya al-Qurazi reports the Prophet's

 ruling in the Banu Qurayza case: those who had grown pubic hair were killed and those who had not were treated as children; the Prophet affirmed Saʿd's judgment.
[THALABI:v3p255/r7] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The two puberty signs specific to women are menstruation and pregnancy.
[THALABI:v3p255/r8] THALABI, d. 427 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | A hadith says a menstruating woman may not pray without a head covering, which the author cites to show that menstruation establishes legal responsibility.
[THALABI:v3p255/r9] THALABI, d. 427 · الشافعي | reports | Al-Shafiʿi defines discernment as uprightness in religion and sound management of property; religious uprightness means avoiding major offenses that invalidate witness standing.
[THALABI:v3p256/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · الحسن وربيعة ومالك | reports | Hasan, Rabiʿa, and Malik define financial competence as avoiding waste, squandering, and grossly bad transactions; they require both financial management and religious uprightness.
[THALABI:v3p256/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · أبو حنيفة وأبو يوسف ومحمد | reports | The three Hanafis say restraint ends once a person is mature, rational, and manages property soundly, whether or not the person is morally upright.
[THALABI:v3p256/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · أبو يوسف ومحمد | reports | Abu Yusuf and Muhammad keep a mature person who mismanages wealth under restraint indefinitely; transactions are void except marriage and emancipation until competence appears.
[THALABI:v3p256/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · أبو حنيفة | reports | Abu Hanifa ends restraint at maturity but withholds the assets of a wastrel until age twenty-five, then transfers them regardless of how they are managed.
[THALABI:v3p256/r5] THALABI, d. 427 · أبو حنيفة | reports | One rationale says the wastrel's transactions remain valid during the withholding period and gives age twenty-five as the time by which he might already be a grandfather.
[THALABI:v3p256/r6] THALABI, d. 427 · أبو حنيفة | reports | Abu Hanifa says the assets are delivered once puberty and sound judgment are established, whether or not the person has married.
[THALABI:v3p256/r7] THALABI, d. 427 · مالك | reports | Malik keeps a discerning adult woman under restraint until marriage and then limits her independent dealings until she is older and experienced, while leaving men unrestricted.
[THALABI:v3p256/r8] THALABI, d. 427 · author | rejects | The author rejects Malik's special restriction on unmarried women: the Prophet accepted women's Eid donations of jewelry without asking marital status or whether husbands consented.
[THALABI:v3p258/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | Guardians must not consume an orphan's property unjustly; isrāf means excess, error, or putting something in the wrong place, as Jarir's poem illustrates.
[THALABI:v3p258/r10] THALABI, d. 427 · النخعي | reports | Al-Nakhaʿi limits the guardian to basic food and clothing, excluding luxury garments and linen.
[THALABI:v3p258/r11] THALABI, d. 427 · الحسن | reports | Hasan and others allow a guardian to consume fruit and milk from the orphan's estate without repayment, but require repayment if he takes gold or silver.
[THALABI:v3p258/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · جرير | reports | Jarir's line uses سرف for error, praising people who give without misplacing or mishandling gifts.
[THALABI:v3p258/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | Guardians must not race to spend an orphan's property before the child grows up and requires it back.
[THALABI:v3p258/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | A wealthy guardian must abstain completely from the orphan's property; ʿiffa means refraining from what is unlawful or improper. | mentions 24:33
[THALABI:v3p258/r5] THALABI, d. 427 · سعيد بن جبير وعبيدة السلماني وأبي العالية وابن عباس | reports | One view reads eating reasonably as borrowing from the orphan's property and repaying when able; if repayment is impossible, no liability remains.
[THALABI:v3p258/r6] THALABI, d. 427 · مجاهد | reports | Mujahid says the guardian may take an advance and invest it in trade, repaying when solvent; Umar's practice is cited as proof.
[THALABI:v3p258/r7] THALABI, d. 427 · عمر بن الخطاب | reports | Umar says he treated public wealth like an orphan's: abstaining when able, taking reasonably when needy, and repaying after becoming solvent.
[THALABI:v3p258/r8] THALABI, d. 427 · الشعبي | reports | Al-Shaʿbi permits consuming the orphan's property only under dire necessity, like eating carrion when compelled.
[THALABI:v3p258/r9] THALABI, d. 427 · عطاء وعكرمة والسدي | reports | Ata, Ikrima, and al-Suddi say reasonable consumption means only taking food with one's fingertips, without overeating or buying clothing from the estate.
[THALABI:v3p259/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · قتادة | reports | Qatada permits a guardian maintaining an orphan's orchard and livestock to take some produce, but forbids consuming the principal assets.
[THALABI:v3p259/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · الضحاك | reports | Al-Dahhak says reasonable benefit means riding the orphan's animal or using a servant, not eating from the estate.
[THALABI:v3p259/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas allows a livestock guardian to drink surplus milk after tending the herd, seeking strays, treating illness, and maintaining its watering place, provided he does not harm the young or overmilk.
[THALABI:v3p259/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · عائشة | reports | Aisha and other scholars say a poor guardian may take compensation proportionate to his care and work, even if it consumes the property, without repayment.
[THALABI:v3p259/r5] THALABI, d. 427 · محمد بن كعب القرظي | reports | Muhammad ibn Kaʿb says the wealthy guardian should abstain, while the needy one may take only the bare minimum as an employee.
[THALABI:v3p259/r6] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | Maʿruf is what is easy and willingly accepted; the author connects the expression with another Qurʾanic reference to fair provision. | mentions 2:236
[THALABI:v3p259/r7] THALABI, d. 427 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Asked whether he may strike an orphan and eat from the estate, the Prophet says to treat him as one's own child and take reasonably without hoarding or using the orphan's property to protect one's own.
[THALABI:v3p259/r8] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | Witnessing the handover is divine guidance, not a duty: it shows the guardian discharged the trust, ends suspicion, and prevents disputes; God is reckoner, judge, and witness.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p452/r12] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | holds | Guardians should test orphans' minds, discernment, and religion before giving them their property.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p452/r13] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | holds | Reaching marriageable age means puberty, by consensus.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p452/r14] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · مجاهد والشعبي | reports | Righteous maturity means sound reason.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p452/r15] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · السدي | reports | Righteous maturity means reason and religious uprightness.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p452/r16] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · ابن عباس والحسن والشافعي | reports | Righteous maturity requires religious uprightness and proper financial management.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p452/r17] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · ابن جريج | reports | Righteous maturity means uprightness and knowledge of what benefits the ward.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p452/r18] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | holds | Once maturity is established, guardians must hand over the property held for the orphans.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p452/r19] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | holds | Guardians must not consume the property extravagantly or hastily before the orphans grow up; excess means exceeding what is lawful.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p452/r20] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · ابن عباس | reports | Acting hastily means consuming an orphan's property before the ward grows up and can take control of it.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p452/r21] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | holds | A wealthy guardian should abstain from using the orphan's property.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p452/r22] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · عمر وابن عباس وجمهور التابعين | reports | A poor guardian may borrow from the orphan and repay it once able.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p452/r23] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · الحسن وإبراهيم ومكحول وقتادة | reports | A poor guardian may take only enough food to satisfy hunger and clothing to cover the body, with no repayment.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p452/r24] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | When Thābit ibn Rifāʿa's uncle asked what he could take from his ward, the Prophet permitted customary consumption without shielding his own property or hoarding the ward's wealth.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p452/r25] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · أبو العالية والشعبي | reports | A poor guardian may eat the orphan's produce and drink livestock milk, but should not take other property such as gold or silver.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p452/r26] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · ابن عباس | reports | A guardian tending orphan camels may drink their milk after caring for strays, sick animals, troughs, and watering, without harming offspring or overmilking.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p452/r27] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · عطاء | reports | A poor guardian may take a fixed wage proportionate to the service provided.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p452/r28] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | In a report about a man with no wealth who cared for an orphan, the Prophet permitted nonwasteful use without shielding one's own property with the ward's.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p452/r29] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | holds | Witness the transfer of the orphans' property so there is evidence that it was handed over.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p452/r30] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | God is sufficient as a witness or as the one who makes witnesses unnecessary.

[WAHIDI-BASIT:v6p328/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · المفسرون | reports | The verse was revealed after Thabit ibn Rifaʿa’s father died and his uncle asked the Prophet when he could use and return the orphan’s property.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v6p328/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · الحسن، وقتادة، ومجاهد، والسدي، وابن زيد | reports | They interpret testing orphans as assessing their intellect and religious conduct.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v6p332/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · ابن عباس | reports | Guardians must not hasten to consume orphans’ property extravagantly before they reach puberty and sound judgment.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v6p332/r10] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | The guardian may not be extravagant and is entitled only to the market-rate wage for his legally assigned work; the wealthy must abstain.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v6p332/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · المفسرون | reports | Guardians may rush to consume the estate out of fear that maturity will require them to hand it over.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v6p332/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | An is accusative as the object of the verbal noun, meaning hastening their maturity.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v6p332/r4] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · ابن عباس | reports | A wealthy guardian must refrain entirely from the orphan’s property.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v6p332/r5] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Istiʿfāf means leaving the property and not eating from it.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v6p332/r6] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · سعيد بن جبير، وعبيدة، ومجاهد، وأبو العالية، وأكثر الروايات عن ابن عباس | reports | A poor guardian may borrow only what he needs, repay upon becoming able, and owes nothing if he dies unable; verse 4:114 supports construing maʿrūf as a loan, as does ʿUmar’s practice. | mentions 4:114
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v6p332/r7] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · عطاء، وعكرمة، والسدي | reports | A poor guardian may take a moderate amount without extravagance and need not repay it.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v6p332/r8] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · إبراهيم | reports | A guardian may take only enough to relieve hunger and cover nakedness.

[WAHIDI-BASIT:v6p336/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Witnessing the transfer protects the guardian with evidence if a dispute arises; it is recommended, not obligatory, and the orphan’s word prevails because the guardian is a trustee.

[WAHIDI-BASIT:v6p336/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · ابن الأنباري | reports | In a threat, ḥasībuhu Allāh means God will hold him accountable; Qays al-Majnūn’s poem uses ḥasīb in that sense.

[WAHIDI-BASIT:v6p336/r5] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | When ḥasīb means sufficient, ḥasībuka Allāh means God is enough for you; compare the phrase in Āl ʿImrān. | mentions 3:173
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v6p336/r6] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · ابن عباس | reports | God is the requiter of both the good and the evildoer, returning to the sense of accounting.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v6p336/r7] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · الزجاج | reports | The prefixed bāʾ in “God is sufficient” constructions is extra, so the meaning is simply that God or the Lord suffices. | mentions 17:17, 17:65, 25:31, 4:45
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v6p336/r8] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Ḥasīban is accusative either as a circumstantial qualifier or as specification distinguishing God from those who suffice or account.

[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#10/r4] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الحسن بن صالح بن حي | reports | Hasan ibn Salih distinguishes the father's appointed guardian, who may take customary support, from a judge's guardian, who may take nothing.
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#10/r5] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · مجاهد | reports | Mujahid says the allowance is abrogated by the prohibition on consuming wealth without trade by mutual consent, because guardianship is not a sale. | mentions 4:29
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#10/r6] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · زيد بن أسلم | reports | Zayd ibn Aslam says the allowance is abrogated by the warning against consuming orphan property unjustly. | mentions 4:10
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#10/r7] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · أبو يوسف | reports | Abu Yusuf says he is unsure whether the allowance was abrogated by the prohibition on consuming wealth without consensual trade.
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#10/r8] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · أبو حنيفة وأبو يوسف ومحمد | reports | A fifth view bars taking from the orphan's principal while the guardian remains at home, but permits necessary expenses when traveling for the orphan, without acquiring property.
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#10/r9] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · أبو قلابة | reports | Abu Qilaba permits consuming from the orphan's profits but not taking liquid capital as a loan or otherwise.
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#11/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الشعبي | reports | Al-Sha'bi compares the guardian's need to necessity for carrion or pork, permitting a limited taking and repayment if able; al-Nahhas says actual necessity already allows taking enough from any available source.
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#11/r2] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · ابن عباس والنخعي | reports | Another Ibn Abbas and al-Nakha'i interpretation tells guardians to live modestly from their own funds so they will not need the orphan's money; al-Nahhas calls this the strongest report because others' property is inviolable without clear proof.
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#11/r3] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الكيا الطبري | prefers | Al-Kiya al-Tabari agrees that the verse requires subsistence from one's own property, not the child's; he harmonizes its ambiguity with clear prohibitions on consuming another's wealth without consent, especially an orphan's. | mentions 4:29, 4:2
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#11/r4] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الكيا الطبري | rejects | Al-Kiya answers that judges' salaries come from unowned public funds, whereas a guardian would take from a specific owner without consent for undefined work and an undefined wage.
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#11/r5] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · أبو العباس | reports | Abu al-Abbas allows fair compensation when a large estate demands substantial work; for a trivial estate he permits only customary small quantities of milk, food, or ghee without harm or excess.
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#12/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | prefers | Al-Qurtubi says abstaining from compensation is better; he condemns fees taken by partition judges and their agents as unlawful and within the threat against consuming orphan property. | mentions 4:10
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#12/r2] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Witnessing the handover is commanded to secure the assets and clear suspicion; scholars differ whether it is recommended, since a guardian is trusted, or obligatory, since he cannot testify in his own favor against heirs.
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#12/r3] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · عمر بن الخطاب وابن جبير | reports | Umar and Ibn Jubayr understand the witnesses to document repayment by a poor guardian of a loan from the orphan's assets.
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#12/r4] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · عبيدة | reports | Ubayda says the verse proves that a guardian who borrowed or consumed the orphan's assets must witness repayment once solvent.
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#12/r5] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | prefers | Al-Qurtubi says the wording covers both repayment and any spending for a ward; witnessing is the apparent command, and a witnessed entrustment is discharged only by witnessed return.
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#12/r6] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The guardian must also protect the orphan's body through discipline and care, just as he safeguards and develops the child's assets; al-Qurtubi discussed this in al-Baqara.
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#13/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · رجل قال للنبي | reports | A man asks whether he may consume an orphan's assets and discipline him; the Prophet allows modest use without accumulating wealth or shielding his own assets, and says to discipline the child as one would one's own.
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#13/r2] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · ابن العربي | reports | Ibn al-Arabi says that although the report is not established with a connected chain, no one can find a way to avoid its ruling.
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#13/r3] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | God is sufficient as accountant of deeds and their recompense, a warning to everyone who denies a right; grammatically the b in billahi is additional and the subject is nominative.
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#2/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The command to test orphans addresses everyone and explains how their property is to be delivered; one occasion reported is the uncle of the orphaned Thabit ibn Rifa'a asking the Prophet what he may use and when to return the child's assets.
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#2/r2] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Testing means assessing character, judgment, and ability to manage property; a promising child may receive a small trial amount, with the full estate delivered if managed well and retained if mismanaged.
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#2/r3] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Passing a test alone does not end guardianship: the verse also requires reaching marriageable age before the estate is released.
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#2/r4] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · جماعة من الفقهاء | reports | Some jurists test a boy by letting him manage household expenses for a month or a small sum under supervision; if he shows sound judgment, the guardian hands over the estate and witnesses it.
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#2/r5] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · جماعة من الفقهاء | reports | For a girl, some jurists test household management, such as supervising cotton workers and judging the yarn; if prudent, her estate is delivered with witnesses, otherwise guardianship continues.
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#2/r6] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الحسن ومجاهد وغيرهما | reports | Hasan, Mujahid, and others say orphans should be tested in intellect, religion, and the growth of their assets.
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#3/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Reaching marriageable age means puberty, as shown by the Quran's parallel phrase about children reaching puberty; puberty can be established by five signs, three shared by both sexes and menstruation and pregnancy specific to women. | mentions 24:59
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#3/r2] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · العلماء | reports | Scholars agree menstruation and pregnancy establish female puberty and trigger legal duties and rulings.
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#3/r3] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الأوزاعي والشافعي وابن حنبل | reports | Al-Awza'i, al-Shafi'i, and Ibn Hanbal, with several Medinese authorities, set puberty at fifteen for someone without a wet dream; legal duties and penalties then apply, and Ibn al-Arabi prefers this limit.
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#3/r4] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · أصبغ بن الفرج | reports | Asbagh says fifteen is the best legal threshold because it is also the age at which a boy receives a share in military service and is allowed into battle.
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#4/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · ابن عمر | reports | Ibn Umar's report supports fifteen as an age threshold: the Prophet accepted him for the Trench at fifteen but had rejected him at Uhud at fourteen.
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#4/r10] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الزهري وعطاء | reports | Al-Zuhri, Ata, al-Shafi'i, and some Malikis say no penalty applies before a wet dream, apparently assigning no legal force to age or pubic hair.
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#4/r11] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · ابن العربي | rejects | Ibn al-Arabi argues that if the Prophet's fifteen-year ruling is not evidence, other proposed ages are unsupported; jurists should use both age and pubic hair, which the Prophet explicitly recognized.
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#4/r2] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · أبو عمر بن عبد البر | reports | For people whose birth dates are unknown, Ibn Abd al-Barr reports Umar's instruction to assess puberty by the appearance of pubic hair; Uthman used a similar sign when judging a boy who stole.
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#4/r3] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · عطية القرظي | reports | Atiyya al-Qurazi says the Prophet inspected Banu Qurayza after Sa'd ibn Mu'adh's ruling, killing those who had grown pubic hair and sparing those who had not; he was spared.

URTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · مالك وأبو حنيفة وغيرهما | reports | Malik, Abu Hanifa, and others set maturity by puberty rather than age; the text gives seventeen years, while Malik also cited a deepened voice and altered nostrils, and Abu Hanifa's best-known view is nineteen for boys and seventeen for girls.
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#4/r5] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · داود | reports | Dawud says age never establishes puberty without a wet dream, even if someone reaches forty.
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#4/r6] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · ابن القاسم وسالم | reports | Ibn al-Qasim, Salim, and several jurists treat pubic hair as a sign of puberty; another Shafi'i view uses that sign specifically in the Banu Qurayza ruling, while green stubble is not enough.
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#4/r7] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · مالك | reports | Malik says his operative practice follows Umar's report: someone on whom the razor passes is legally mature for punishment.
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#4/r8] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · أصبغ | reports | Asbagh prefers imposing a penalty only when both pubic hair and puberty are established.
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#4/r9] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · أبو حنيفة | reports | Abu Hanifa rejects pubic hair as either proof or indication of puberty.
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#5/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | rejects | Al-Qurtubi notes that Ibn al-Arabi took the opposite position in al-Anfal, reading Ibn Umar's report as distinguishing those able to fight and receive spoils from dependants; Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz understood it similarly.
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#5/r10] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · أبو حنيفة وزفر بن الهذيل والنخعي | reports | Abu Hanifa, Zufar, and al-Nakha'i say a free adult cannot be placed under guardianship once he reaches manhood, even if profligate, so long as he is rational.
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#5/r2] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Anistu means perceived or saw, as in Moses seeing a fire; al-Azhari explains the idiom as looking to see whether anyone is there, and al-Nabigha's wild bull poem illustrates watchful looking. | mentions 28:29
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#5/r3] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The verb can also mean sensed, found, or knew; its underlying sense is seeing.
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#5/r4] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · السلمي وعيسى والثقفي وابن مسعود | reports | The common reading has rushdan with a damma on ra and silent shin; al-Sulami, Isa, al-Thaqafi, and Ibn Masud read it with both vowels open, two dialectal forms and possible verbal nouns.
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#5/r5] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الحسن وقتادة وغيرهما | reports | Hasan, Qatada, and others interpret rushd as soundness of intellect and religion.
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#5/r6] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · ابن عباس والسدي والثوري | reports | Ibn Abbas, al-Suddi, and al-Thawri define sound judgment as competence of mind and preservation of wealth.
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#5/r7] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · سعيد بن جبير والشعبي | reports | Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Sha'bi say even an old person should not receive an orphan's estate until prudence is observed; al-Dahhak likewise withholds it even at a hundred absent sound management.
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#5/r8] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · مجاهد | reports | Mujahid says rushd refers specifically to intellect.
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#5/r9] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · أكثر العلماء | reports | Most scholars, including Malik, say sound judgment follows puberty; a person who remains imprudent stays under guardianship even when old.
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#6/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · قتادة | reports | Qatada transmits the case of Habban ibn Munqidh, whose weak commercial judgment prompted a request for interdiction; the Prophet instead told him to state that there was no fraud and that he had three days to withdraw.
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#6/r2] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | rejects | The case does not prove that guardianship is forbidden, because it was specific to Habban, as al-Qurtubi explained under al-Baqara.
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#7/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الشافعي | reports | Al-Shafi'i interdicts someone who corrupts both wealth and religion or wealth alone; if religion is corrupt but wealth managed, one view interdicts him and another does not.
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#7/r2] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · أبو العباس بن شريح | reports | Ibn Shurayh chooses the Shafi'i view that a person who misuses religion but manages wealth should still be interdicted.
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#7/r3] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · أبو إسحاق المروزي | prefers | Al-Maruzi chooses not to interdict someone who is religiously corrupt but manages wealth; al-Qurtubi calls this the apparent Shafi'i position.
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#7/r4] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الثعلبي | reports | Al-Tha'labi attributes the permissibility of interdicting a spendthrift to Uthman, Ali, al-Zubayr, Aisha, Ibn Abbas, Abd Allah ibn Ja'far, Shurayh, and many jurists, and reports a claim of consensus.
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#7/r5] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Property is delivered only when both sound judgment and puberty are present; most jurists agree, while Abu Hanifa, Zufar, and al-Nakha'i release a person at twenty-five without requiring sound judgment.
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#7/r6] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · علماؤنا | reports | Maliki scholars require a girl to have consummated marriage after puberty before testing her judgment, reasoning that seclusion limits her experience; men encounter public dealings from childhood.
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#7/r7] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | prefers | Al-Qurtubi prefers al-Shafi'i's view that intercourse itself adds nothing to a woman's judgment if she already understands affairs and manages her wealth.
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#7/r8] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · ابن العربي | rejects | Ibn al-Arabi reports Maliki waiting periods of five to seven years for a girl with a father and one year for an orphan, but says these limits lack evidence and are difficult to define; the Quranic criterion is demonstrated judgment suited to each person.
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#7/r9] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | rejects | Al-Qurtubi criticizes Abu Hanifa's grandfather rationale and Abu Bakr al-Razi's argument from two verses: unrestricted wording must, by agreement among legal theorists, be read with the qualified wording.
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#8/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Once a girl is prudent, contracts made during the waiting period are treated either as void until then or as valid only when sound judgment is shown; after it, they are accepted unless folly appears.
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#8/r2] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · ابن عطية | prefers | Views differ on whether a guardian must obtain a judge's confirmation before release; Ibn Atiyya says guardians today should, given collusion and false declarations of a ward's prudence.
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#8/r3] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | prefers | Malik and one Shafi'i view restore guardianship if a released person becomes wasteful; Abu Hanifa says it cannot return, but al-Qurtubi cites the Quran's protection of wealth and its provision for a guardian when a debtor becomes foolish or weak. | mentions 4:5, 2:282
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#8/r4] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | A guardian may manage an orphan's estate as a father would: trade, pay zakat and obligations, cover damages and parents' support, arrange marriage, pay a dowry, acquire a concubine, and settle claims in the ward's interest.
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#8/r5] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | A guardian who pays some creditors from an estate is not liable if funds sufficient for the remaining debts are later lost; if he knowingly distributes the whole estate despite other debts, he must make up the other creditors' shares.
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#8/r6] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | A guardian who pays a deceased person's debt without witnesses is liable; if payment was witnessed but the witnesses later die after a long time, he is not liable.
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#9/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Al-Qurtubi points back to al-Baqara 2:220 for fuller rulings on guardians' spending and other fiduciary duties.
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#9/r2] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The prohibition does not imply that non-extravagant consumption is allowed; it forbids consuming the orphan's property except what is specifically permitted. Israf means excess or transgression.
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#9/r3] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The Arabic word israf is explained as excess, crossing a limit, erroneous spending, waste, or heedlessness; poems illustrate the word's usage.
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#9/r4] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Badaran means rushing to consume before an orphan reaches maturity; grammatically it is coordinated with israfan, and an yakbaru is governed by badaran.
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#9/r5] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | A wealthy guardian must refrain from the orphan's funds, while a poor guardian may consume customary support; isti'faf means abstaining, as in the command to unmarried people. | mentions 24:33
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#9/r6] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | A poor guardian who has an orphan may consume from the child's assets only without excess, waste, or accumulating principal.
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#9/r7] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · عائشة | reports | Aisha says the allowance applies to a needy guardian who cares for and improves the orphan's affairs; one narration limits it proportionately to the estate.
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#9/r8] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · ربيعة ويحيى بن سعيد | reports | Rabi'a and Yahya ibn Sa'id instead take the verse to mean that the orphan receives support according to whether his own assets are ample or limited; al-Qurtubi says the majority view is correct because the child cannot manage his money.
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6#9/r9] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · عمر بن الخطاب وابن عباس وعبيدة وابن جبير والشعبي ومجاهد وأبو العالية | reports | One view lets an impoverished guardian borrow customary support and repay it when solvent; Umar compared his use of public funds to a guardian's use of an orphan's property.

L:4:6/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The Prophet told Hind to take enough customary support for herself and her child; another report about a son asking to be fed indicates this applies to one unable to earn.
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6/r2] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Someone who has reached puberty is expected to seek a livelihood, since the verse sets reaching marriageable age as a threshold.

[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6/r5] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | reports | An alternative takes the address as directed to the orphan's guardian, who should spend according to the child's means and needs; if the child has no property, the state and then closest Muslims, especially the mother, must care for him without reimbursement. | mentions 2:233
[QURTUBI-FULL:4:6/r6] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Speaking kindly means gentle address and reassuring promises; interpretations include prayers for the child and promising delivery of the estate once he is prudent.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:4:6/r1] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | Test orphans before puberty by observing religious soundness and money management, letting them handle preliminary contract steps; Abu Hanifa instead tests by giving them something to manage.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:4:6/r10] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | Witness the transfer to prove receipt and prevent suspicion, dispute, and liability; the chosen position and Malik require proof from the guardian, unlike Abu Hanifa.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:4:6/r11] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | God suffices as accountant; guardians must not violate the command or exceed its limits.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:4:6/r2] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | Puberty occurs by wet dream or at fifteen years according to this school, supported by a prophetic report on recording liability and applying penalties; Abu Hanifa sets eighteen.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:4:6/r3] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · أبو حنيفة | reports | Abu Hanifa sets puberty at eighteen; bulūgh al-nikāḥ euphemistically means maturity and suitability for marriage in his view.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:4:6/r4] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | Ānastum means perceiving maturity; a reading aḥsastum has the sense of perceiving.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:4:6/r5] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | Deliver property promptly at puberty only if maturity is observed; the conditional grammar makes maturity a prerequisite.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:4:6/r6] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · أبو حنيفة | reports | Abu Hanifa gives property after seven years beyond puberty even without observed maturity, since it is a period of change when a child begins to discern and is ordered to worship.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:4:6/r7] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | Guardians must not consume orphan wealth wastefully or hastily before the children grow; this may describe the guardian's own extravagance and haste.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:4:6/r8] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | A wealthy guardian abstains; a poor guardian may take a customary amount proportionate to need and work, since the language implies a limited right in the child's property.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:4:6/r9] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · النبي | reports | The Prophet told an orphan's guardian to take fairly without accumulating wealth or shielding his own property with the orphan's.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p204#2/r1] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Test orphans' understanding and ability to manage property before puberty by letting them handle it; this supports a discerning child's permission to trade.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p204#2/r10] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | reports | Ḥasīb means one who audits and reckons; alternatively, it warns the guardian taking a customary share not to exceed it because God will account for it.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p204#2/r2] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Reaching marriage means puberty, when a person becomes fit for marriage and its purpose of procreation.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p204#2/r3] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Anīsū means they have discerned sound judgment in handling business and transactions.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p204#2/r4] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Once puberty and discernible judgment are present, deliver their property without delay; the syntax makes release conditional on judgment after puberty.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p204#2/r5] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | The indefinite رشد either specifies commercial judgment or signals that even a little sound judgment suffices; this supports Abū Ḥanīfa's release of property at age twenty-five.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p204#2/r6] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Do not consume the property wastefully or rush to spend it before the orphans grow up and reclaim it; the verbal nouns are circumstantial or purposive.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p204#2/r7] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | A rich guardian must refrain from the orphan's property; a poor guardian may take a carefully measured customary amount.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p204#2/r8] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · إبراهيم | reports | Ibrāhīm defines a poor guardian's customary share as enough to fill hunger and cover nakedness.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p204#2/r9] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | When returning the property, obtain witnesses to prove receipt and avoid denial or a disputed oath.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p491/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | Ānasa means to perceive or sense; al-Farra glosses it as finding, al-Zajjaj as knowing, Ata as seeing, and Ibn Abbas as recognizing, close in meaning.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p518/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | One occasion report says Rifa'a died leaving the young Thabit, whose guardian asked what use of the estate was lawful and when it should be handed over.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p518/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | Another account says Aws b. Thabit or Aws b. Suwayd died leaving Umm Kujja, three daughters, and two cousins, who seized the estate and excluded the women.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p518/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | In pre-Islamic custom, women, daughters, and young boys did not inherit; Umm Kujja complained, and male relatives argued her sons could not fight or carry burdens, so the Prophet awaited revelation.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p518/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن عباس، السدي، مقاتل، سفيان | reports | They define testing orphans as testing their judgment; al-Tha'labi adds judgment, religion, care of property, and sound management.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p518/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | A boy can be tested with a small amount of money under supervision; a girl can be entrusted with household work and managing wool production, payments, and receipt.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p518/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Testing should suit each child's abilities and work; after puberty, if maturity appears, the estate is handed over and witnessed, with witnessing following delivery.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p519/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The maturity that must be observed is the maturity made a condition in the verse.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p519/r10] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | حتى marks the end of testing, introduces إذا, and the response to إذا is فإن آنستم, followed by the response to إن, فادفعوا; maturity is observed after puberty.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p519/r11] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | Some grammarians say the clause after حتى is genitive; most say حتى governs nothing, as in poetic examples beginning وحتى.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p519/r12] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | بلغوا النكاح elliptically means reaching the age or time for marriage.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p519/r13] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن عباس، عطاء، الفراء، الزجاج | reports | They gloss آنستم as knew, saw, found, and knew, respectively; these meanings are close.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p519/r14] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن مسعود | reports | Ibn Masud reads فإن أحستم, deleting the medial radical from أحسستم; the deletion is rare, though others report it as the dialect of Sulaym and productive with some attached pronouns.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p519/r15] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن مسعود، أبو عبد الرحمن، أبو السمال، عيسى الثقفي | reports | They read رشدا with fatḥa on both letters; an anomalous reading has ḍamma on both.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p519/r16] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | رشدا is indefinite because it means a kind or aspect of maturity; one need not wait for complete maturity.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p519/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن سيرين | reports | Ibn Sirin would wait a year after maturity testing, so the child experiences all four seasons before transfer.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p519/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The verse does not specify the legal age or the signs of puberty; juristic works discuss those questions.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p519/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الجمهور | reports | The apparent rule, adopted by the majority, keeps an immature person under restraint indefinitely and withholds the estate.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p519/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · النخعي، أبو حنيفة | reports | Al-Nakha'i and Abu Hanifa wait until age twenty-five, then release the property whether discernment is evident or not.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p519/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The apparent wording gives the guardian independent authority to hand over the estate.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p519/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · طائفة | reports | Some require the guardian to present the case to a judge and establ

[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p519/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The general word orphans includes daughters, who therefore receive the same treatment as sons.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p519/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | Reported daughter-specific waiting rules include maturity without marriage, five years after consummation, a year, or seven years with a father versus one year for an orphan without a guardian.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p520#2/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | A poem about giving generously describes the gifts as containing no miserliness or waste, illustrating proper spending.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p520#2/r10] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · أبو حنيفة وصاحباه | reports | Abu Hanifa and his two companions allow a guardian who is traveling to take what he needs but not to retain anything; a resident may take nothing.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p520#2/r11] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الشعبي | reports | Al-Sha'bi permits taking only in dire need, like eating carrion, and requires repayment when able; travel or residence alone makes no difference.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p520#2/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن عباس وغيره | reports | They say rushing means the guardian hastens to exploit the ward's estate before the ward matures, claiming to act before the child can take it back.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p520#2/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | إسرافا and بدارا may be circumstantial verbal nouns or reasons; بدار can suggest a race between the child growing and guardian taking property, or the guardian alone, and أن يكبروا may be the object of the verbal noun or express fear.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p520#2/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The apparent division addresses the guardian: a rich guardian should refrain, while a poor guardian may take only modest food carefully assessed.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p520#2/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · إبراهيم، عطاء، الحسن، قتادة | reports | They say the reasonable amount is a modest allowance for necessities; no liability attaches and it need not be repaid if the guardian later becomes solvent, a view followed by jurists.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p520#2/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · عمر، ابن عباس، عبيدة، الشعبي، أبو العالية، ابن جبير | reports | They require repayment once solvent and forbid borrowing beyond need; al-Awzai also holds this view.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p520#2/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن عباس، أبو العالية، الحسن، الشعبي | reports | They limit reasonable use to small customary amounts of milk or dates and prohibit taking the principal assets.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p520#2/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · طائفة، الإمام أحمد | reports | Some say reasonable means compensation proportionate to the guardian's service; one report attributes this to Ahmad.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p520#2/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الحسن بن حي | reports | Hasan b. Hayy distinguishes a father-appointed guardian, who may eat reasonably, from a judge-appointed guardian, who must seek wages from the public treasury.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p520/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن عطية، مالك | reports | Ibn Atiyya and Malik require both puberty and discernment before property is handed over.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p520/r10] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The prohibition on consuming or wasting the estate is an independent sentence, not coordinated with the command to hand it over, which follows the puberty condition.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p520/r11] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | rejects | Reading the prohibition as coordinated with فادفعوا would create a hardship by conditioning it on puberty; neither the wording nor its opposite makes eating otherwise lawful.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p520/r12] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | إسراف is excessive spending, and سرف is error in where one spends.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p520/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · أبو حنيفة | reports | Abu Hanifa considers either condition sufficient unless folly is known, comparing this to the rule for concubinage.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p520/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | rejects | The analogy fails: puberty is not stated as a cause of transfer but marks the usual age when judgment matures; discernment is tested then, as shown by إذا for timing and إن for the condition.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p520/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · سيبويه | reports | Sibawayh allows إذا to function as a conditional particle in poetry under necessity because it needs a response and is followed by a verb.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p520/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalil argues إذا is not itself conditional because what follows is expected to happen: one says one will come when dates redden, not if they redden.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p520/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | rejects | Abu Hayyan rejects the claim that إذا lacks conditional sense: grammarians broadly treat it as a future adverb usually carrying conditional meaning, even though it does not govern jussive mood.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p520/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · مالك | reports | If a person becomes mature and then returns to foolishness, Malik says the restriction is reinstated.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p520/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · أبو حنيفة | reports | Abu Hanifa says a restriction is not reinstated after maturity; the two views are also reported from al-Shafi'i.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p520/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Eating here stands for taking property because consumption is the main use of what is taken.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p522#2/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | If a guardian takes something that is not a wage, jurists further dispute whether it becomes a debt repayable upon solvency.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p522#2/r10] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن عباس، السدي، مقاتل | reports | They gloss حسيبا as a witness.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p522#2/r11] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | حسيب may be a reciprocal intensive noun or a strengthened active participle; grammarians also disagree whether كفى is a verb or a noun of action and whether its subject is Allah or an implicit مصدر.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p522#2/r12] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The sound parse makes كفى a verb with Allah as subject and an extra ب; an alternative requires the Kufan allowance for an implicit verbal noun to govern its complement, which Basrans reject.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p522#2/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | فليستعفف is more emphatic than فليعف because it asks for increased restraint.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p522#2/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Witnessing delivery prevents disputes and suspicion, protects the guardian from liability if the ward denies receipt, reassures the ward, and marks release from restraint for ordinary dealings.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p522#2/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · أبو حنيفة وأصحابه، مالك | reports | If there are no witnesses and the ward accuses the guardian, these authorities accept the guardian's statement with an oath.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p522#2/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الشافعي | reports | Al-Shafi'i requires the guardian to produce evidence if he did not witness the transfer.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p522#2/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The apparent wording makes witnessing obligatory, though some say it is recommended.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p522#2/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · عمرو بن جبير | reports | Amr b. Jubayr limits witnessing to repayment by a guardian of money borrowed from an orphan while poor and repaid after becoming solvent.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p522#2/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | Other interpretations say the verse requires witnessing repayment of anything taken from the orphan, or documenting expenditures on the ward so a later dispute can be resolved; a trust received with witnesses is discharged only by witnessed return.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p522#2/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الأعمش، الطبري | reports | They explain حسيبا as sufficient to testify, from a verb meaning to suffice; other senses are one who reckons or accounts for deeds and recompenses them, warning against lying.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p522/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · مجاهد | reports | Mujahid says the permission to eat is abrogated by the warning against devouring orphan property in 4:10. | mentions 4:10
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p522/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · أبو يوسف | reports | Abu Yusuf suggests the permission may be abrogated by the ban on consuming one another's property wrongfully in 2:188, so a guardian may take neither loan nor other payment. | mentions 2:188
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p522/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن عباس، النخعي | reports | They say this is about the guardian's own wealth: the wealthy should be self-sufficient and the poor should manage their own assets rather than need the orphan's property; al-Kiya al-Tabari chooses this view among Shafi'is.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p522/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | Some allow a wage from a large estate when managing it occupies the guardian's time; with little work, nothing is due, though modest customary food may be given without harm.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p522/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ربيعة، يحيى بن سعيد | reports | They say the verse divides the orphans' circumstances rather than guardians': spend frugally from a wealthy ward's estate and according to a poor ward's means, with guardians addressed indirectly.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p522/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The disagreements concern whether the division describes guardian or child; whether it concerns the guardian's or child's property; abrogation; the type of taking, eligible guardians, permissible items, wages, and repayment.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p522/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الشعبي | reports | The necessity-only view allows only enough as with carrion, requires repayment if possible, and applies whether the guardian is traveling or at home.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p523/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | حسيبا may be accusative as specifi

[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p531/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | It repeats key words and meanings: fear, creation, orphan, women, inheritance, and guarding against injustice.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p531/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The matching forms in “hand over” and “when you hand over” create perfect paronomasia.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p531/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The added force in فليستعفف intensifies the meaning of seeking restraint.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:6#2/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The indefinite rushdan indicates variety: any kind of maturity is sufficient.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:6#2/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Most read rushdan with ḍamma and sukūn; Ibn Masud and al-Sulami read fatḥa on both consonants, and some read two ḍammas.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:6#2/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Ānasa means to sense or perceive; al-Farraʾ also glosses it as ‘find,’ and another view is ‘see.’
[SAMIN-DURR:4:6#2/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | ‘Wastefully and hastily’ may be two objects of purpose, describing why guardians consume the property.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:6#2/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas says guardians hurried to consume orphans’ wealth before the child grew up and took the property back.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:6#2/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Alternatively, both accusatives are circumstantial: the guardian acts wastefully and in haste.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:6#2/r7] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Badāran is the verbal noun of bādara; it may describe mutual haste by guardian and orphan, or a one-sided action with form III meaning form I.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:6#3/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | ‘That they grow up’ may be the object of badār, as a verbal noun governs its object; the cited ‘feeding an orphan’ verse is parallel, though this government is disputed. | mentions 90:14-15
[SAMIN-DURR:4:6#3/r10] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الزجاج | reports | Al-Zajjaj says the bāʾ enters the subject because the utterance conveys a command, but the author finds this contradictory about whether bāʾ is extra and who the subject is.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:6#3/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Alternatively, an implied ‘fearing’ makes the clause a purpose, with the object of badār omitted.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:6#3/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | prefers | The prohibition begins an independent sentence; coordinating it with the conditional answer is rejected because it would make the warning precede the event it depends on.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:6#3/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | rejects | The alternative coordination would make ‘do not consume’ follow the conditional result, contradicting ‘in haste lest they grow up.’
[SAMIN-DURR:4:6#3/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | prefers | Kafā is a verb, not a noun-like particle; its subject is the noun governed by the extra bāʾ.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:6#3/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · أبو البقاء | reports | Abu al-Baqa says the extra bāʾ signals the imperative sense ‘be content with God.’
[SAMIN-DURR:4:6#3/r7] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · ابن السراج | reports | Ibn al-Sarraj instead posits an implicit verbal-noun subject, ‘sufficiency,’ with bi-Allah as its semantic object; the author notes Basrans allow this only in poetic necessity.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:6#3/r8] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الشيخ | reports | The Shaykh rejects the hidden verbal-noun analysis because it leaves an omitted subject and makes an omitted noun govern its complement.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:6#3/r9] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | rejects | The author responds that if the subject is implicit, bi-Allah need not attach to that subject; it can attach to the verb, as Makki and al-Zajjaj suggest.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:6#4/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · ابن عطية | reports | Ibn Atiyya says bi-Allah is nominative after an extra preposition and that the preposition gives a statement the force of a command; the author sees this as answering al-Zajjaj by making the bāʾ extra.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:6#4/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · ابن عيسى | reports | Ibn ʿIsa says bāʾ joins the phrase as both subject-like and genitive attachment, reflecting that divine sufficiency exceeds ordinary sufficiency; the author says this needs thought.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:6#4/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | prefers | Ḥasīban is most likely an accusative of specification, shown by its ability to take min; the alternative is a circumstantial accusative.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:6#4/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Here kafā takes one object, omitted as ‘God suffices you.’
[SAMIN-DURR:4:6#4/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · أبو البقاء | reports | Abu al-Baqa treats kafā as taking two omitted objects, ‘God suffices you against them,’ citing 2:137; the author says that is a different sense and questions the analysis. | mentions 2:137
[SAMIN-DURR:4:6/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Most grammarians make ḥattā a conjunction marking the endpoint of testing: test orphans until puberty, then give them their wealth if they show maturity.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:6/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الزجاج وابن درستويه | reports | Al-Zajjaj, Ibn Darastawayh, and others instead make ḥattā a preposition, leaving idhā purely temporal rather than conditional.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:6/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | On the majority analysis, idhā is governed by the sense of its answer: when they reach marriageable age mature, hand over their property.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:6/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Some deny that idhā is conditional because its event is expected to occur; Sibawayh allows it to govern a condition in poetry, while al-Khalil argues from ‘when the dates ripen’ versus ‘if they ripen.’
[SAMIN-DURR:4:6/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الشيخ | reports | The Shaykh explains that grammarians agree idhā usually carries conditional meaning; denials mean only that it does not govern jussive verbs.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:6/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | rejects | The author says there is no need to insert ‘the age’ or ‘the time’ of marriage: the wording means they become fit for marriage.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:6/r7] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The fāʾ in ‘if you perceive’ answers idhā, and the fāʾ in ‘then hand over’ answers in.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:6/r8] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · ابن مسعود | reports | Ibn Masud reads aḥastum, with one of the two identical sīn letters deleted from aḥsastum; the deletion is irregular, though some report it as a productive Sulaymi dialect rule.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:6/r9] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · أبو زبيد | reports | Abu Zubayd’s poem supplies a parallel for deleting one sīn from a doubled verb.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p215/r1] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, al-Hasan, al-Suddi, and Muqatil ibn Hayyan say guardians should test the orphans before handing over their wealth.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p215/r2] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · مجاهد | reports | Mujahid glosses reaching marriageable age as reaching puberty.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p215/r3] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | Most scholars say a boy reaches puberty through a wet dream and emission of semen capable of producing a child.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p215/r4] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · علي بن أبي طالب | reports | Ali quotes the Prophet: legal orphanhood ends at puberty, and a fast is not to be maintained in silence until night.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p215/r5] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Aisha and other Companions report that legal responsibility is lifted from a child until puberty, a sleeper until waking, and an insane person until recovery; fifteen is also treated as adulthood from Ibn Umar's battle-age report, which Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz called the distinction between child and adult.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p215/r6] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · عمر بن عبد العزيز | reports | Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz treated Ibn Umar's admission to battle at fifteen, after rejection at fourteen, as the distinction between minor and adult.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p215/r7] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · ابن كثير | prefers | Of three views on pubic hair as a sign of puberty, Ibn Kathir rejects distinguishing Muslim boys from protected non-Muslim boys and holds the sign applies to both because it is natural and artificial removal is unlikely.

[ALUSI-FULL:v4p205/r12] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The contrast between idha for puberty and in for maturity reflects certainty of the former and uncertainty of the latter.

[ALUSI-FULL:v4p205/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · أبو زيد الطائي | reports | Abu Zayd al-Taʾi’s verse supplies evidence for the dialectal treatment of a doubled verb with a pronoun.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p205/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | Rushd means financial discernment and prudent management, or, in another view, religious rectitude as well as sound financial judgment.

[ALUSI-FULL:v4p206/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | rejects | Critics argue that if any maturity inevitably appears by twenty-five, Abu Hanifa’s position collapses into the other imams’ rule; al-Alusi says financial competence need not arise by that age, while generic maturity would not satisfy the verse.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p206/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الفخر | reports | Al-Fakhr says the test concerns protecting property, so the required maturity is competence in managing its interests; otherwise the verse’s clauses would be disconnected.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p206/r5] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الفخر | reports | Al-Fakhr’s clear analogy says an adult or elder without the reason needed to preserve and use property should remain barred from it just as a child is.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p206/r6] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | rejects | Al-Alusi condemns Ibn Hazm and his Shiʿi followers for vilifying Abu Hanifa over this subsidiary disagreement while often relying on weaker evidence elsewhere.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p207#2/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Israf is exceeding what is permitted, by excess or shortfall; asrafa usually names excess and sarafa deficiency, while heedlessness or error is not intended here.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p207#2/r10] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | The poor guardian may eat from the property only according to recognized custom and to the necessary amount for food and clothing, as ʿAtaʾ and Qatada say.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p207#2/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Mubadara means haste: the guardian may rush to consume the property before the orphan grows, while the orphan may hasten to reclaim it; the word is linked to fullness.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p207#2/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The etymological examples are the full moon, a money bag filled with money, and a grain heap filled with food.

[ALUSI-FULL:v4p207/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Al-Alusi defends Abu Hanifa: once an orphan reaches adulthood, he is accountable for belief, worship, choice, reward, and punishment, so keeping his property under another’s control resembles oppression.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p207/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Although this reasoning might warrant immediate payment at puberty even without competence, payment is delayed until twenty-five to allow education, maturity, and restraint from waste.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p207/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The delay resembles, in one respect, holding the property of rebels until they return to obedience.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p207/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Seven years was chosen because it commonly changes a child’s capacities; ten also marks change in the prayer hadith, but the lower sufficient period is adopted.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p207/r5] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | rejects | Al-Alusi denies that the restriction turns on every kind of foolishness or remains in force indefinitely; the relevant condition is childish incapacity and the legal school does not infer absence of consequence automatically from absence of a condition.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p207/r6] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | prefers | The warning against consuming orphan property wastefully and before they grow supports Abu Hanifa’s view that property should not be withheld once they have grown, with the special delay for an immature adult explained earlier.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p208/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · ابن عباس | reports | A poor guardian may take from an orphan's assets in proportion to the work and benefit he provides, without extravagance or waste.

[ALUSI-FULL:v4p208/r11] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الشافعية والمالكية | reports | The Shafi'i and Maliki schools regard witnessing the transfer as obligatory and infer that a guardian cannot prove delivery merely by his assertion.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p208/r12] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · السدي | reports | Al-Suddi interprets God's sufficiency as witness for the parties.

[ALUSI-FULL:v4p208/r14] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Alternatively, God suffices as your reckoner, so do not disobey the command or exceed its limits; this is apt because trustees are accountable for what they hold.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p208/r15] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · أبو البقاء | reports | Abu al-Baqa analyzes 'God suffices' either with God as subject and an extra ba conveying command, or with an implicit subject and God as object; hasiban is circumstantial or specification.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p208/r16] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · السمين | reports | Al-Samin treats kafa as taking one object, while Abu al-Baqa allows two, with the implied sense of God sparing you harm or the like.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p208/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | In answer to Ibn Umar, the Prophet permitted eating from an orphan's wealth without extravagance, accumulating wealth, or using it to shield one's own assets.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p208/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Whether the guardian's permitted consumption counts as wages has two opinions; the author's school takes the second, as al-Jassas states in al-Ahkam.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p208/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · سعيد بن جبير ومجاهد وأبي العالية والزهري وعبيدة السلماني والباقر | reports | A poor guardian may borrow enough from the orphan's property for his needs and repay it once able; this is the recognized manner of eating.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p208/r5] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · عمر بن الخطاب | reports | Umar treated the public treasury like an orphan's property: he abstained when wealthy, took a reasonable amount when needy, and repaid it when able.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p208/r6] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas, on the authority of Ata, says the permission was abrogated by the warning against consuming orphan property wrongfully. | mentions 4:10
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p208/r7] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · عكرمة عن ابن عباس | reports | One reported view permits a poor guardian to take food from the orphan's wealth but not clothing.

[ALUSI-FULL:v4p208/r9] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The handover clause addresses guardians and trustees: after observing the preceding requirements, they deliver the assets under their care to the orphans; fronting the recipient emphasizes them.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p209#2/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Perfect shaykhs are charged to appoint successors and authorize disciples who are fit to guide others.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p209#2/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Not consuming the disciples' wealth means not benefiting from their spiritual gifts to their exclusion or rushing before they mature into guidance; this is a grave disease of the ego.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p209#2/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | A spiritually rich guardian should abstain from a disciple's resources; one unable to bear need may benefit only to necessity's measure.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p209#2/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | A spiritual handover calls for witnessing God and the spirits of the divine presence and taking a covenant that the disciple honor rights owed to God and creation.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p209#2/r5] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | God is true existence and sees hidden betrayals and inward secrets; He is the sufficient protector.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p209/r15] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Testing the orphans signifies testing deficient wayfarers; reaching marriage means becoming ready for guidance, and sound judgment means steadiness on the path without fickleness.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p209/r16] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Handing over the wealth means entrusting spiritual secrets only to free and worthy people.

[IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p242/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Choosing anistum rather than alimtum suggests that property should be handed over as soon as the first sign of sound judgment is known, without delay.

[IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p242/r4] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · اللخمي | reports | A guardian appointed by a father or judge should not be accepted as having certified the ward's maturity without investigation, given possible collusion and corruption.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p242/r5] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · ابن عطية | reports | Ibn Atiyya likewise calls for court confirmation of a ward's sound judgment because guardians may collude with an immature ward to secure their own release.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p242/r6] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Although this caution did not become general practice, notaries commend documenting maturity for a father's appointee; the sound view for a judge's appointee requires proof before the judge, as practiced.

[IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p243/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | By analogy, a person who becomes foolish as an adult or loses reason through illness or old-age senility is also placed under guardianship because the cause persists; Abu Hanifa disagrees.

[IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p243/r7] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · الجصاص | rejects | Al-Jassas argues that the indefinite noun permits any kind of judgment, including mere reason, so sound financial management is unnecessary; the author rejects this as bad Arabic and a category error.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p243/r8] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The property is attributed to the orphans because their claim becomes firmly established once mature, when their disposal no longer threatens relatives' and the community's interests.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p244#2/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Permission for a poor guardian to eat customarily qualifies the general ban: a modest share supports the guardian so that earning a livelihood does not distract from managing the ward's assets. | mentions 4:2
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p244#2/r10] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · أبو حنيفة وصاحباه | reports | Abu Hanifa and his two companions allow taking only when traveling on the ward's business, and only for travel sustenance.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p244#2/r11] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · الجمهور | prefers | The majority equate a judge-appointed guardian with a father's guardian; the author endorses this because the verse does not distinguish them.

[IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p244#2/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · النبي | reports | A man who said he was poor and owned nothing was told to take from his orphan ward's property without extravagance, haste, or accumulating wealth.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p244#2/r4] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · عائشة | reports | A report in Sahih Muslim says the verse concerns a needy orphan's guardian eating from the estate in reasonable proportion.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p244#2/r5] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · المالكية | reports | The Malikis set the guardian's customary allowance at the equivalent wage for comparable work.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p244#2/r6] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · عمر بن الخطاب وابن عباس وأبو عبيدة وابن جبير والشعبي ومجاهد | reports | These authorities say the permission is only a loan; Umar compared himself to a guardian over public funds and would repay after becoming able.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p244#2/r7] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · عطاء وإبراهيم | reports | Ata and Ibrahim hold that a guardian need not repay what he took if he later becomes solvent.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p244#2/r8] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · الحسن والشعبي وابن عباس | reports | Another report permits a guardian to drink the ward's milk, eat fruit, treat a diseased camel, and repair its watering trough.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p244#2/r9] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · عكرمة وابن عباس والشعبي | reports | They interpret the permission as applying only in dire necessity, like eating carrion; the author calls this the weakest view because the verse hinges on poverty and the ward's property, whereas necessity concerns any property.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p244/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The prohibition reiterates the earlier ban in 4:2 and exposes guardians who hasten to consume wards' assets before the wards mature and can demand an accounting. | mentions 4:2
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p244/r2] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | At revelation, assets were often livestock, dates, grain, and wool; guardians consumed them by lavishly spending on themselves and their households rather than hiding or transferring them.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p244/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Israf means excessive spending on pleasures; its accusative may be circumstantial or stand for an absolute object, and the point is to censure the manner of consumption, not limit the ban to lavish eating.
